4.3 Is the pattern real? A shuffle comparison

TODO: Make at least one “shuffle comparison”. Randomly permute (shuffle) your outcome variable so that any real relationship is destroyed, then plot the real data next to a few shuffled copies. If the real panel looks clearly different from the shuffled ones, your pattern is unlikely to be random noise.

Code 
# TODO: Create your shuffle comparison (see the EXAMPLE below).

TODO: Interpret the shuffle comparison.

NoteEXAMPLE: exploratory plots and a shuffle comparison (delete this block)
Code 
tooth <- ToothGrowth |>
  mutate(dose = factor(dose), supp = factor(supp, labels = c("Orange juice", "Ascorbic acid")))

ggplot(tooth, aes(x = dose, y = len, fill = supp)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length", fill = "Supplement")

Interpretation: Tooth length rises steadily with dose for both supplements. At 0.5 and 1 mg/day, orange juice seems to give longer teeth than ascorbic acid, but the boxes overlap at 2 mg/day. This motivates Hypothesis 2 (dose effect and interaction) and Hypothesis 1 (supplement effect).

Code 
# Shuffle the outcome within five copies of the data, then add the real data.
shuffled <- map(1:5, \(i) tooth |> mutate(len = sample(len), panel = paste("Shuffled", i))) |>
  list_rbind()
lineup <- bind_rows(tooth |> mutate(panel = "Real data"), shuffled) |>
  mutate(panel = fct_relevel(panel, "Real data"))

ggplot(lineup, aes(x = dose, y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length")

Interpretation: Only the real-data panel shows a clear upward trend with dose. The shuffled panels look flat. This suggests the dose pattern is not just random variation, so it is worth testing formally.

NoteEXAMPLE: reporting results (delete this block)

Hypothesis 1: Welch two-sample t-test.

Code 
h1 <- t.test(len ~ supp, data = tooth)  # Welch: does not assume equal variances
h1

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  len by supp
t = 1.9153, df = 55.309, p-value = 0.06063
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Orange juice and group Ascorbic acid is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.1710156  7.5710156
sample estimates:
 mean in group Orange juice mean in group Ascorbic acid 
                   20.66333                    16.96333

Result: The mean tooth length was 20.7 for orange juice and 17 for ascorbic acid, t(55.3) = 1.92, p = 0.061, 95% CI for the difference [-0.17, 7.57]. Because p > 0.05 and the interval includes 0, we fail to reject H0. Averaged over all doses, the data do not show a clear difference between the supplements.

Hypothesis 2: two-way ANOVA with interaction.

Code 
h2 <- aov(len ~ dose * supp, data = tooth)
summary(h2)
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
dose         2 2426.4  1213.2  92.000  < 2e-16 ***
supp         1  205.4   205.4  15.572 0.000231 ***
dose:supp    2  108.3    54.2   4.107 0.021860 *  
Residuals   54  712.1    13.2                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
Code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(h2, which = 1:2)  # residuals vs fitted (equal variance), Q-Q (normality)

Result: Dose, supplement and their interaction are all significant (p < 0.05), so we reject H0. The residual plots show roughly constant spread and approximately normal residuals, so the ANOVA assumptions are reasonable. Notice that supplement type is significant once dose is taken into account, even though the simple t-test in Hypothesis 1 was not. Controlling for another variable can change a conclusion.

## EXAMPLE: exploratory plots and a shuffle comparison (delete this block)

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Tooth length by vitamin C dose and supplement type (n = 60)."

tooth <- ToothGrowth |>
  mutate(dose = factor(dose), supp = factor(supp, labels = c("Orange juice", "Ascorbic acid")))

ggplot(tooth, aes(x = dose, y = len, fill = supp)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15), alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length", fill = "Supplement")
```

*Interpretation:* Tooth length rises steadily with dose for both supplements.
At 0.5 and 1 mg/day, orange juice seems to give longer teeth than ascorbic acid,
but the boxes overlap at 2 mg/day. This motivates Hypothesis 2 (dose effect and
interaction) and Hypothesis 1 (supplement effect).

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-shuffle
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Real data (top left) compared with five copies in which tooth length was randomly shuffled."
#| fig-height: 5

# Shuffle the outcome within five copies of the data, then add the real data.
shuffled <- map(1:5, \(i) tooth |> mutate(len = sample(len), panel = paste("Shuffled", i))) |>
  list_rbind()
lineup <- bind_rows(tooth |> mutate(panel = "Real data"), shuffled) |>
  mutate(panel = fct_relevel(panel, "Real data"))

ggplot(lineup, aes(x = dose, y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey85") +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length")
```

*Interpretation:* Only the real-data panel shows a clear upward trend with dose.
The shuffled panels look flat. This suggests the dose pattern is not just
random variation, so it is worth testing formally.
:::

and `r round(h1$estimate[2], 1)` for ascorbic acid,
t(`r round(h1$parameter, 1)`) = `r round(h1$statistic, 2)`,
p = `r signif(h1$p.value, 2)`, 95% CI for the difference
[`r round(h1$conf.int[1], 2)`, `r round(h1$conf.int[2], 2)`].
Because p > 0.05 and the interval includes 0, we **fail to reject H~0~**.
Averaged over all doses, the data do not show a clear difference between the
supplements.

**Hypothesis 2: two-way ANOVA with interaction.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-example-h2
#| fig-cap: "EXAMPLE: Residual diagnostics for the two-way ANOVA."
#| fig-height: 4

h2 <- aov(len ~ dose * supp, data = tooth)
summary(h2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(h2, which = 1:2)  # residuals vs fitted (equal variance), Q-Q (normality)
```

*Result:* Dose, supplement and their interaction are all significant
(p < 0.05), so we **reject H~0~**. The residual plots show roughly constant
spread and approximately normal residuals, so the ANOVA assumptions are
reasonable. Notice that supplement type *is* significant once dose is taken
into account, even though the simple t-test in Hypothesis 1 was not. Controlling
for another variable can change a conclusion.
:::
